title: 2 Chronicles 3:8–17
context: The unit describes the most holy place, its gold, the cherubim, the veil, and the two pillars set before the house. The inner room is twenty cubits by twenty, matching the plan of 1 Kings 6:16–20, and is overlaid with six hundred talents of fine gold. The cherubim’s wings span twenty cubits, five cubits to the wall and five to the other cherub on each side, and they stand facing toward the house. A veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen, ornamented with cherubim, is named here; 1 Kings 6:31–32 describes doors of olive wood for the inner sanctuary rather than this veil. The two accounts should be reported side by side, not forced into a single furnishing. Before the house stand two pillars “thirty-five cubits high,” with capitals of five cubits; 1 Kings 7:15–16 gives pillars “eighteen cubits high apiece” and capitals of five cubits. The already drafted 1 Kings 7:15 notes in this worktree already record the Chronicles height as a difference left unharmonized. The pillars are named Jachin and Boaz, as in 1 Kings 7:21. Both traditions keep the whole description as building report, refuse to allegorize the measures, the veil, or the names, and invent no party contrast over the figures that do not agree.

verses.text: He made the most holy place. Its length, according to the width of the house, was twenty cubits, and its width twenty cubits; and he overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents.
verses.arminianNotes:
He made “the most holy place.” “Its length, according to the width of the house, was twenty cubits, and its width twenty cubits; and he overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents.” The twenty-by-twenty plan agrees with 1 Kings 6, which also makes the inner sanctuary twenty cubits, and in that book twenty cubits high as well. This verse does not state the height, and it adds the six hundred talents of gold. The talent is a large weight; the notes do not press a modern figure as if the verse had given one, and they do not treat the gold as a symbol.

Arminian readers take the room as a measured, overlaid sanctuary, matching 1 Kings 6 in plan, without reading a doctrine out of the talent count.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the agreement and the added weight. Twenty cubits by twenty cubits is the shared plan; six hundred talents is this verse’s notice, left as a quantity of gold, not as a code.

Both traditions refuse to allegorize the most holy place or to fill in the missing height from the other book as if it had been written here.

verses.text: The weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. He overlaid the upper rooms with gold.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. He overlaid the upper rooms with gold.” The verse gives a weight for the nails and extends the overlay to the upper rooms. The shekel is a standard weight in the narrative; no more exact modern equivalent is needed to read the line, and the nails are not turned into a type.

Arminian readers take the fifty shekels and the upper rooms as part of the same gold work, a construction detail, not a hidden lesson.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stay descriptive. Nails of gold and overlaid upper rooms belong to the finish of the house, set beside the six hundred talents of 3:8 without a symbolic system.

Both traditions leave the verse as a report of materials and weight.

verses.text: In the most holy place he made two cherubim by carving, and they overlaid them with gold.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the most holy place he made two cherubim by carving, and they overlaid them with gold.” The cherubim are carved work, then covered with gold, standing in the inner room just described. 1 Kings 6:23–28 also places two olive-wood cherubim, overlaid with gold, in the inner sanctuary, with related but not identical wording.

Arminian readers take the two figures as real furnishings of the most holy place, carved and gilded, not as a puzzle in images.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the 1 Kings 6 parallel and keep the wording of this verse. They are made by carving and overlaid with gold, a report, not an allegory of later doctrine.

Both traditions refuse to press the cherubim beyond what the following verses measure.

verses.text: The wings of the cherubim were twenty cubits long: the wing of the one was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house; and the other wing was five cubits, reaching to the wing of the other cherub.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The wings of the cherubim were twenty cubits long: the wing of the one was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house; and the other wing was five cubits, reaching to the wing of the other cherub.” The span fills the twenty-cubit width of the room, five cubits to the wall and five to the other cherub. 1 Kings 6:24–27 gives the same five-cubit wings and a span that reaches across the house. The numbers describe placement, not a spiritual code.

Arminian readers read the measures as the way the two figures occupy the room, wing to wall and wing to wing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the cubits as architecture. Twenty cubits of wing, five and five, match the width already given for the most holy place.

Both traditions leave the description unallegorized and unforced against 1 Kings 6.

verses.text: The wing of the other cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house; and the other wing was five cubits, joining to the wing of the other cherub.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The wing of the other cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house; and the other wing was five cubits, joining to the wing of the other cherub.” The second figure is measured in the same way, so that the two sets of wings meet in the middle and reach the walls. The verse completes the picture begun in 3:11.

Arminian readers take the repeated five cubits as the matching side of the same arrangement, a careful report of the pair.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a symmetrical description, wall to wing and wing to wing, still in the register of the room’s furnishings.

Both traditions keep the measures as measures and invent no contrast over the repetition.

verses.text: The wings of these cherubim spread themselves out twenty cubits. They stood on their feet, and their faces were toward the house.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The wings of these cherubim spread themselves out twenty cubits. They stood on their feet, and their faces were toward the house.” The total span is restated, and the stance is given: they stand, and they face toward the house, that is, toward the larger room. 1 Kings 6:27–28 is related but does not state the faces in this way.

Arminian readers take the posture and the facing as part of the furnishing, not as a cue for a typological reading of the inner room.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stay with the wording. The wings fill twenty cubits; the cherubim stand on their feet and look toward the house.

Both traditions refuse to allegorize the faces or the span.

verses.text: He made the veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen, and ornamented it with cherubim.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He made the veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen, and ornamented it with cherubim.” This book names a veil at the inner sanctuary, colored and worked with cherubim. 1 Kings 6:31–32 describes doors of olive wood, carved with cherubim, palm trees, and flowers, and overlaid with gold, rather than this veil. The two furnishings should be named as the two books give them, not reduced to one.

Arminian readers report the veil here and the doors in 1 Kings 6, without deciding that one account must cancel the other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers do the same. Blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen, ornamented with cherubim, is this verse’s notice; the olive-wood doors belong to 1 Kings 6.

Both traditions leave the difference unharmonized and do not turn the veil into a later doctrinal symbol the verse does not name.

verses.text: Also he made before the house two pillars thirty-five cubits high, and the capital that was on the top of each of them was five cubits.
verses.arminianNotes:
He made before the house “two pillars thirty-five cubits high, and the capital that was on the top of each of them was five cubits.” 1 Kings 7:15–16 says he fashioned “two pillars of bronze, eighteen cubits high apiece”; and that each capital was five cubits. The capital height agrees; the pillar height does not. The already drafted 1 Kings 7:15 notes record this Chronicles figure and leave it unharmonized, also noting other eighteen-cubit notices in the later fall of the city.

Arminian readers name thirty-five cubits here and eighteen cubits in 1 Kings 7:15, and they refuse to hide either number or to invent a solution the verses do not give.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stay consistent with those Kings notes. Five cubits for the capitals is shared; thirty-five and eighteen are different heights and are not to be forced into one measure.

Both traditions treat the difference as a reported one, not as a theological fork, and they do not allegorize the pillars.

verses.text: He made chains in the inner sanctuary, and put them on the tops of the pillars; and he made one hundred pomegranates, and put them on the chains.
verses.arminianNotes:
He made “chains in the inner sanctuary,” put them on the tops of the pillars, and made “one hundred pomegranates,” set on the chains. 1 Kings 7:17–20 describes network, chain work, and pomegranates on the capitals in more detail, including different counts in places. The ornaments should be read as decoration of the pillars, not as a code, and the two descriptions should not be forced into one inventory.

Arminian readers take the chains and the hundred pomegranates as the finish named in this verse, beside the fuller account in 1 Kings 7.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the two ornament lists unmerged. Chains and pomegranates belong to the capitals in both books; the wording and some counts differ.

Both traditions keep the verse descriptive and refuse allegory.

verses.text: He set up the pillars before the temple, one on the right hand and the other on the left; and called the name of that on the right hand Jachin, and the name of that on the left Boaz.
verses.arminianNotes:
He set up the pillars “before the temple, one on the right hand and the other on the left; and called the name of that on the right hand Jachin, and the name of that on the left Boaz.” The names agree with 1 Kings 7:21, which also sets a right pillar called Jachin and a left called Boaz. The meanings of the names are not given in this verse, and they should not be turned into a doctrinal system here.

Arminian readers take the naming as the close of the unit, two named pillars before the temple, matching 1 Kings 7:21 in the names and the sides.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep Jachin and Boaz as the names the two books share, and they refuse to allegorize the pillars or to invent a contrast over them.

Both traditions close the chapter on that shared naming, with the height difference of 3:15 still left as it stands.
